content: Fatty liver disease is a condition characterized by the accumulation of fat within liver cells, accompanied by inflammation of the liver. The term steatohepatitis is derived from steato, meaning fat, and hepatitis, meaning inflammation of the liver. This condition is classically associated with excessive alcohol consumption but is also frequently observed in individuals with diabetes and obesity. When fatty liver disease occurs in the absence of significant alcohol intake, it is referred to as non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH). Both alcoholic and non-alcoholic steatohepatitis can progress to cirrhosis, and NASH is now recognized as a common cause of unexplained cirrhosis. Despite its prevalence, the management of fatty liver disease remains suboptimal among healthcare providers. Fatty liver disease involves the fatty degeneration of parenchymal liver cells, which leads to a yellow discoloration of the liver. This condition is reversible and is characterized by the accumulation of large vacuoles of triglyceride fat within liver cells, a process known as steatosis. Although fatty liver disease has multiple causes, it can be considered a single disease entity that occurs globally in individuals with excessive alcohol consumption or obesity, with or without insulin resistance. Additionally, fatty liver disease is associated with other medical conditions that affect fat metabolism. Morphologically, it is challenging to distinguish alcoholic fatty liver disease from non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, as both conditions exhibit microvesicular and macrovesicular fatty changes at various stages. Fatty liver disease is prevalent in 10% to 24% of the general population across different countries. Among obese individuals, the prevalence increases significantly, affecting up to 75% of this population. Of these, approximately 35% will develop non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) despite no evidence of excessive alcohol consumption. In the United States, fatty liver disease is the most common cause of abnormal liver function tests. African Americans and Mexican Americans exhibit higher rates of unexplained serum aminotransferase elevations compared to whites, although the prevalence of fatty liver disease across different racial groups remains unclear. Most individuals with fatty liver disease are asymptomatic, and the condition is often discovered incidentally during evaluations for abnormal liver function tests or hepatomegaly noted in unrelated medical conditions. Elevated liver biochemistry is observed in approximately 50% of patients with simple steatosis. In non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, serum alanine aminotransferase (ALT) levels are typically higher than aspartate aminotransferase (AST) levels, whereas the opposite pattern is seen in alcoholic fatty liver disease. The treatment of fatty liver disease depends on addressing the underlying cause. Early intervention targeting the root cause can reverse the process of steatosis. Recent studies suggest that lifestyle modifications, including dietary changes and exercise, as well as the use of antidiabetic medications, may alter the disease's progression. For instance, a randomized controlled trial demonstrated that pioglitazone led to both metabolic and histological improvements in patients with non-alcoholic steatohepatitis. Preventive measures for fatty liver disease include avoiding excessive alcohol consumption, maintaining a healthy diet, and achieving a healthy weight. These strategies are essential in reducing the risk of developing fatty liver disease.
